Eggs of the Blue-billed curassow (Crax alberti) incubated under controlled conditions at a core temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C] typically hatch after a period of 32 days [ab = 32 days], a value inferred from development rates in the congeneric Red-billed curassow (Crax blumenbachii). Upon hatching, the precocial chicks emerge with a body mass averaging just 200 grams [Ww0 = 200 grams], an advantage that allows them to begin following the hen within hours. This initial wet weight is meager relative to the ultimate mass these birds will achieve and underscores the intense growth phase that lies ahead. The survival and growth of these downy young depend critically on the thermal environment provided by the attending parent, as they are unable to effectively thermoregulate during their first days of life. The 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C] incubation temperature is therefore essential for normal embryonic development, and deviations from this value can lead to extended incubation periods or reduced hatchling viability in captive breeding programs.

Female Blue-billed curassows attain a definitive adult body mass of 2800 grams [Wwi = 2800 grams], a substantial size that places them among the larger members of the Cracidae family. This ultimate wet weight for females is not reached until well after the juvenile period, as the birds undergo a prolonged phase of somatic growth. In contrast, males are somewhat larger on average, though specific mass data for males remain scarce in the literature. During the energetically demanding breeding season, females must maintain this high body mass while investing considerable resources into egg production. A typical clutch consists of only two eggs, and field observations indicate that a female will produce just a single clutch each year, yielding a maximum reproductive rate of 2 eggs per year [Ri = 2 eggs per year] when maintained at the typical body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This exceedingly low reproductive rate is characteristic of many large-bodied tropical birds and is likely an adaptation to the stable but resource-limited environment of the lowland forests they inhabit. The energetic cost of producing even two large, yolk-rich eggs is substantial, and the prolonged period of parental care further constrains annual fecundity.

Under the warm thermal conditions typical of their active metabolic state, which hover near 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], the developmental biology of Crax alberti reveals a compressed early life history relative to other large galliforms. The young curassow achieves fledging—defined here as the age at which it can attain sustained flight—at merely 5 days after hatching [tx = 5 days after hatching], a remarkably short nestling period that underscores the precocial nature of this species at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. Even before this rapid achievement of flight capability, the chicks are highly mobile and begin foraging alongside the adult female almost immediately. This abbreviated dependency phase, inferred from developmental studies of the Red-billed curassow, likely serves as a critical anti-predator adaptation in a forest environment where ground nests and helpless young are especially vulnerable. Although the chicks can fly at this early age, they continue to be brooded by the female at night and remain under her watchful guidance for several additional weeks before achieving complete independence from parental oversight.

Basal metabolic rate measurements conducted on resting adult Blue-billed curassows at their typical body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C] reveal a maximum oxygen consumption of 1186.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 1186.5 milliliters per hour]. This value reflects the high energetic cost of maintaining endothermy in a large-bodied tropical bird and is consistent with general allometric relationships for cracids. The metabolic machinery required to sustain this oxygen consumption supports not only basal maintenance but also the considerable muscular activity involved in foraging and predator evasion. Interestingly, this resting metabolic rate is measured at the same temperature (40.7 °C) that governs the developmental rates of the embryo and the timing of early life history events, suggesting a fundamental thermal constraint operating across multiple life stages. The efficiency of the metabolic machinery that sustains an incubation period that is prolonged relative to smaller galliforms ultimately determines the species' ability to thrive in its environment.

An assessment of lifespan from captive records indicates that the Blue-billed curassow can achieve a maximum longevity of approximately 22.8 years [am = approximately 22.8 years] when maintained under the stable thermal conditions of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], a lifespan comparable to other large cracids and reflecting the slow life-history pace typical of tropical forest-dwelling birds that face low extrinsic mortality rates. This extended lifespan is accompanied by a notably delayed onset of reproductive activity. Puberty, defined as the time since birth at sexual maturation, is reached at 152.5 days after birth [tp = 152.5 days after birth], a developmental milestone that, like the timing of hatching and fledging, has been estimated from the closely related Red-billed curassow at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. Following the attainment of sexual maturity, the first brood is not produced until considerably later, with a time since birth at first brood of approximately 2.1 years [tR = approximately 2.1 years]. at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]This substantial gap between reaching puberty and initiating reproduction likely reflects the need for young birds to secure a territory and establish a pair bond within the dense forest habitat. The combination of a leisurely maturation schedule and the production of just a single clutch of two eggs annually underscores the species' vulnerability to population decline in the face of habitat loss and hunting pressure.
